content.content:
1	Pipework in process plants, buildings, vehicles and drilling installations often has to be gripped by a device that cannot be threaded on from a free end of the pipe. Sensors, monitoring heads, marking tools, small actuators and conduit supports are attached to a run of pipe that is already installed. A clamp intended for that duty is therefore built as a split clamp: a frame that opens, is placed around the pipe transversely, and is closed again.
2	
3	A split frame presents a mechanical problem that a one piece collar does not have, because the tightening motion has to be delivered to a frame that is divided. Where the grip is obtained by drawing the two frame halves toward one another so that the frame itself shrinks onto the pipe, the closing force enters the frame at the split line, and the grip that results depends on the closure hardware and on how far the halves have been drawn together.
4	
5	Where instead the frame is fitted with jaws that are advanced against the pipe one at a time, the grip is taken away from the split line, but the jaws have to be balanced against one another by the operator. If one jaw is advanced further than the others, the pipe is pushed away from the axis of the frame, and the clamp is seated differently each time it is fitted.
6	
7	A clamp whose jaw faces match one nominal pipe diameter also obliges a technician to select the clamp to suit the pipe before working, and a jaw face of fixed curvature meets a pipe of a different diameter along an edge rather than over an area.
8	
9	An operator working with a quick acting latch further has little indication of how hard the clamp has been applied. The latch closes to the same position whether the jaws have only just reached the pipe or have been driven hard against it, so the feel of the latch does not report the load the clamp is carrying, and a reading of pipe diameter reports only the size of the pipe.
10	
11	There is accordingly a need for a split pipe clamp that can be fitted by hand around an in place pipe over a range of diameters, that advances several jaws onto the pipe together rather than one at a time, and that reports mechanically to the operator when the clamping load has reached the intended range.
12

Pipework in process plants, buildings, vehicles and drilling installations often has to be gripped by a device that cannot be threaded on from a free end of the pipe. Sensors, monitoring heads, marking tools, small actuators and conduit supports are attached to a run of pipe that is already installed. A clamp intended for that duty is therefore built as a split clamp: a frame that opens, is placed around the pipe transversely, and is closed again.

A split frame presents a mechanical problem that a one piece collar does not have, because the tightening motion has to be delivered to a frame that is divided. Where the grip is obtained by drawing the two frame halves toward one another so that the frame itself shrinks onto the pipe, the closing force enters the frame at the split line, and the grip that results depends on the closure hardware and on how far the halves have been drawn together.

Where instead the frame is fitted with jaws that are advanced against the pipe one at a time, the grip is taken away from the split line, but the jaws have to be balanced against one another by the operator. If one jaw is advanced further than the others, the pipe is pushed away from the axis of the frame, and the clamp is seated differently each time it is fitted.

A clamp whose jaw faces match one nominal pipe diameter also obliges a technician to select the clamp to suit the pipe before working, and a jaw face of fixed curvature meets a pipe of a different diameter along an edge rather than over an area.

An operator working with a quick acting latch further has little indication of how hard the clamp has been applied. The latch closes to the same position whether the jaws have only just reached the pipe or have been driven hard against it, so the feel of the latch does not report the load the clamp is carrying, and a reading of pipe diameter reports only the size of the pipe.

There is accordingly a need for a split pipe clamp that can be fitted by hand around an in place pipe over a range of diameters, that advances several jaws onto the pipe together rather than one at a time, and that reports mechanically to the operator when the clamping load has reached the intended range.

1	In the following description, like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views. The described arrangement is one form of the invention and is not a limitation on the scope of the claims. Terms of orientation such as inward, outward, radial and circumferential are used with reference to a central axis of the closed frame, which in use is substantially coincident with the axis of the pipe being gripped.
2	
3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	Referring to FIG. 1, a split pipe clamp 10 comprises a first frame half 12 and a second frame half 14. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are each substantially semicircular, and together they define a frame that surrounds a pipe 20 when closed. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are joined at a hinge end of the frame by a hinge 16 and are releasably joined at a latch end of the frame, opposite the hinge end, by a releasable latch 18. Swinging the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16 opens the frame laterally, so that the split pipe clamp 10 can be placed around the pipe 20. The split pipe clamp 10 and the pipe 20 together form an installed clamp assembly when the split pipe clamp 10 is closed and clamped on the pipe 20.
6	
7	Three jaw carriages 22 are distributed circumferentially about the closed frame, as shown in FIG. 1.
8	
9	The frame carries a mounting boss 66. The mounting boss 66 supports a sensor, a tool or a conduit on the split pipe clamp 10. The mounting boss 66 does not participate in synchronizing the jaw carriages 22.
10	
11	Jaw carriages and jaw pads
12	
13	Referring to FIG. 2, each jaw carriage 22 is slidable in a respective radial guide 24 of the frame. The radial guide 24 constrains the jaw carriage 22 to travel along a radial path toward and away from the central axis of the closed frame.
14	
15	Each jaw carriage 22 carries a jaw pad 26 that is mounted on the jaw carriage 22 for pivoting movement and that presents a concave bearing surface toward the central axis of the closed frame. Because the jaw pad 26 pivots relative to the jaw carriage 22, the jaw pad 26 bears on the pipe 20 without requiring a tool specific pipe diameter.
16	
17	A carriage spring 42 biases each jaw carriage 22 outward, away from the central axis of the closed frame. When the releasable latch 18 is released, the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22 outward and lift the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened.
18	
19	The segmented cam ring
20	
21	A cam ring 30 is retained in an annular guide 36 of the frame. The annular guide 36, shown in FIG. 2, retains the cam ring 30 while allowing the cam ring 30 to rotate through a limited stroke about the central axis of the closed frame.
22	
23	The mounting boss 66 stands on the frame outside the annular guide 36, as shown in FIG. 2.
24	
25	The cam ring 30 is segmented. Referring to FIG. 3, the cam ring 30 comprises a first cam-ring segment 32 and a second cam-ring segment 34. The first cam-ring segment 32 is carried by the first frame half 12 and the second cam-ring segment 34 is carried by the second frame half 14, each segment being retained by the frame half that carries it. Each segment accordingly stays with its own frame half when the frame is opened, and the frame halves can be swung apart without dismantling the drive.
26	
27	The first cam-ring segment 32 has a first hinge-end drive face 44 and a first latch-end drive face 48. The second cam-ring segment 34 has a second hinge-end drive face 46 and a second latch-end drive face 50. The first hinge-end drive face 44 and the second hinge-end drive face 46 are complementary to one another, and the first latch-end drive face 48 and the second latch-end drive face 50 are complementary to one another. Closing the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 brings the first hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the second hinge-end drive face 46 at the hinge end and brings the first latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the second latch-end drive face 50 at the latch end, and thereby couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 so that they rotate together as one cam ring 30 about the central axis of the closed frame.
28	
29	In the closed frame each pair of complementary drive faces transmits circumferential drive from one cam-ring segment to the other, and the complementary drive faces separate when the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are swung apart about the hinge 16.
30	
31	Each jaw carriage 22 carries a follower 40 that is received in a respective oblique slot 38 of the cam ring 30. The follower 40 and the oblique slot 38 are shown in FIG. 2. Each oblique slot 38 is inclined to the circumferential direction of the cam ring 30, so that rotation of the cam ring 30 through the limited stroke displaces the follower 40, and with it the jaw carriage 22, along the radial guide 24. The oblique slots 38 are arranged so that rotation of the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke produces the same inward travel at every jaw carriage 22. The inward travel of the three jaw carriages 22 is thereby synchronized.
32	
33	The latch drive
34	
35	The releasable latch 18 carries a wedge 52, as shown in FIG. 4. Moving the releasable latch 18 drives the wedge 52 against a ring drive face 54 of the cam ring 30, shown in FIG. 3, and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke.
36	
37	The releasable latch 18 has a first position and a second position. In the first position the releasable latch 18 holds the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 around the pipe 20 without clamping the pipe 20. The second position is an over-center position, in which the releasable latch 18 has driven the wedge 52 and the cam ring 30 and clamps the pipe 20.
38	
39	Referring again to FIG. 4, the releasable latch 18 comprises a latch handle 56, a latch housing 58 and a force-limiting spring stack 62. The force-limiting spring stack 62 lies in a drive path between the latch handle 56 and the wedge 52.
40	
41	Once all of the jaw pads 26 have contacted the pipe 20, further movement of the latch handle 56 toward the over-center position compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62 rather than forcing one jaw pad 26 farther than the others. The latch travel that remains after contact is therefore taken up by the force-limiting spring stack 62.
42	
43	An indicator pin 64 is visible on the releasable latch 18 and moves relative to a fixed edge 60 of the latch housing 58 when the force-limiting spring stack 62 enters a predetermined compression range. The position of the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60 is a mechanical report that the split pipe clamp 10 is loaded within that range. The indicator pin 64 reports clamp loading and does not measure the diameter of the pipe 20.
44	
45	Installation and removal
46	
47	To install the split pipe clamp 10, an operator opens the releasable latch 18 and swings the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 20 and closes them, which brings the first hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the second hinge-end drive face 46 and the first latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the second latch-end drive face 50, and so couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 into a single cam ring 30. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the first position, in which the frame halves are held around the pipe 20 without clamping. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the over-center position. The wedge 52 bears on the ring drive face 54 and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke, the oblique slots 38 advance all of the jaw carriages 22 inward together, and the jaw pads 26 pivot and seat on the pipe 20. Latch travel remaining after the jaw pads 26 seat compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62, and the operator observes the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60.
48	
49	To remove the split pipe clamp 10, the operator releases the releasable latch 18. The force-limiting spring stack 62 unloads and the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22, lifting the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are then swung apart about the hinge 16, and the first hinge-end drive face 44, the second hinge-end drive face 46, the first latch-end drive face 48 and the second latch-end drive face 50 separate so that the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 travel with their own frame halves. The split pipe clamp 10 is reusable.
50

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a split pipe clamp 10 comprises a first frame half 12 and a second frame half 14. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are each substantially semicircular, and together they define a frame that surrounds a pipe 20 when closed. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are joined at a hinge end of the frame by a hinge 16 and are releasably joined at a latch end of the frame, opposite the hinge end, by a releasable latch 18. Swinging the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16 opens the frame laterally, so that the split pipe clamp 10 can be placed around the pipe 20. The split pipe clamp 10 and the pipe 20 together form an installed clamp assembly when the split pipe clamp 10 is closed and clamped on the pipe 20.

Three jaw carriages 22 are distributed circumferentially about the closed frame, as shown in FIG. 1.

The frame carries a mounting boss 66. The mounting boss 66 supports a sensor, a tool or a conduit on the split pipe clamp 10. The mounting boss 66 does not participate in synchronizing the jaw carriages 22.

Jaw carriages and jaw pads

Referring to FIG. 2, each jaw carriage 22 is slidable in a respective radial guide 24 of the frame. The radial guide 24 constrains the jaw carriage 22 to travel along a radial path toward and away from the central axis of the closed frame.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a jaw pad 26 that is mounted on the jaw carriage 22 for pivoting movement and that presents a concave bearing surface toward the central axis of the closed frame. Because the jaw pad 26 pivots relative to the jaw carriage 22, the jaw pad 26 bears on the pipe 20 without requiring a tool specific pipe diameter.

A carriage spring 42 biases each jaw carriage 22 outward, away from the central axis of the closed frame. When the releasable latch 18 is released, the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22 outward and lift the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened.

The segmented cam ring

A cam ring 30 is retained in an annular guide 36 of the frame. The annular guide 36, shown in FIG. 2, retains the cam ring 30 while allowing the cam ring 30 to rotate through a limited stroke about the central axis of the closed frame.

The mounting boss 66 stands on the frame outside the annular guide 36, as shown in FIG. 2.

The cam ring 30 is segmented. Referring to FIG. 3, the cam ring 30 comprises a first cam-ring segment 32 and a second cam-ring segment 34. The first cam-ring segment 32 is carried by the first frame half 12 and the second cam-ring segment 34 is carried by the second frame half 14, each segment being retained by the frame half that carries it. Each segment accordingly stays with its own frame half when the frame is opened, and the frame halves can be swung apart without dismantling the drive.

The first cam-ring segment 32 has a first hinge-end drive face 44 and a first latch-end drive face 48. The second cam-ring segment 34 has a second hinge-end drive face 46 and a second latch-end drive face 50. The first hinge-end drive face 44 and the second hinge-end drive face 46 are complementary to one another, and the first latch-end drive face 48 and the second latch-end drive face 50 are complementary to one another. Closing the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 brings the first hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the second hinge-end drive face 46 at the hinge end and brings the first latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the second latch-end drive face 50 at the latch end, and thereby couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 so that they rotate together as one cam ring 30 about the central axis of the closed frame.

In the closed frame each pair of complementary drive faces transmits circumferential drive from one cam-ring segment to the other, and the complementary drive faces separate when the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are swung apart about the hinge 16.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a follower 40 that is received in a respective oblique slot 38 of the cam ring 30. The follower 40 and the oblique slot 38 are shown in FIG. 2. Each oblique slot 38 is inclined to the circumferential direction of the cam ring 30, so that rotation of the cam ring 30 through the limited stroke displaces the follower 40, and with it the jaw carriage 22, along the radial guide 24. The oblique slots 38 are arranged so that rotation of the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke produces the same inward travel at every jaw carriage 22. The inward travel of the three jaw carriages 22 is thereby synchronized.

The latch drive

The releasable latch 18 carries a wedge 52, as shown in FIG. 4. Moving the releasable latch 18 drives the wedge 52 against a ring drive face 54 of the cam ring 30, shown in FIG. 3, and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke.

The releasable latch 18 has a first position and a second position. In the first position the releasable latch 18 holds the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 around the pipe 20 without clamping the pipe 20. The second position is an over-center position, in which the releasable latch 18 has driven the wedge 52 and the cam ring 30 and clamps the pipe 20.

Referring again to FIG. 4, the releasable latch 18 comprises a latch handle 56, a latch housing 58 and a force-limiting spring stack 62. The force-limiting spring stack 62 lies in a drive path between the latch handle 56 and the wedge 52.

Once all of the jaw pads 26 have contacted the pipe 20, further movement of the latch handle 56 toward the over-center position compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62 rather than forcing one jaw pad 26 farther than the others. The latch travel that remains after contact is therefore taken up by the force-limiting spring stack 62.

An indicator pin 64 is visible on the releasable latch 18 and moves relative to a fixed edge 60 of the latch housing 58 when the force-limiting spring stack 62 enters a predetermined compression range. The position of the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60 is a mechanical report that the split pipe clamp 10 is loaded within that range. The indicator pin 64 reports clamp loading and does not measure the diameter of the pipe 20.

Installation and removal

To install the split pipe clamp 10, an operator opens the releasable latch 18 and swings the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 20 and closes them, which brings the first hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the second hinge-end drive face 46 and the first latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the second latch-end drive face 50, and so couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 into a single cam ring 30. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the first position, in which the frame halves are held around the pipe 20 without clamping. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the over-center position. The wedge 52 bears on the ring drive face 54 and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke, the oblique slots 38 advance all of the jaw carriages 22 inward together, and the jaw pads 26 pivot and seat on the pipe 20. Latch travel remaining after the jaw pads 26 seat compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62, and the operator observes the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60.

To remove the split pipe clamp 10, the operator releases the releasable latch 18. The force-limiting spring stack 62 unloads and the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22, lifting the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are then swung apart about the hinge 16, and the first hinge-end drive face 44, the second hinge-end drive face 46, the first latch-end drive face 48 and the second latch-end drive face 50 separate so that the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 travel with their own frame halves. The split pipe clamp 10 is reusable.

The essential relationship of the arrangement described here is that closure of the frame halves couples the cam-ring segments, that travel of the releasable latch 18 drives the coupled cam ring 30, that the oblique slots 38 synchronize the radial travel of the jaw carriages 22, and that the force-limiting spring stack 62 accommodates the remaining latch travel. The features described above may be combined in ways other than those expressly set out, and modifications within the understanding of a person skilled in the art fall within the scope of the claims that follow.

1	Pipework in process plants, buildings, vehicles and drilling installations often has to be gripped by a device that cannot be threaded on from a free end of the pipe. Sensors, monitoring heads, marking tools, small actuators and conduit supports are attached to a run of pipe that is already installed. A clamp intended for that duty is therefore built as a split clamp: a frame that opens, is placed around the pipe transversely, and is closed again.
2	
3	A split frame presents a mechanical problem that a one piece collar does not have, because the tightening motion has to be delivered to a frame that is divided. Where the grip is obtained by drawing the two frame halves toward one another so that the frame itself shrinks onto the pipe, the closing force enters the frame at the split line, and the grip that results depends on the closure hardware and on how far the halves have been drawn together.
4	
5	Where instead the frame is fitted with jaws that are advanced against the pipe one at a time, the grip is taken away from the split line, but the jaws have to be balanced against one another by the operator. If one jaw is advanced further than the others, the pipe is pushed away from the axis of the frame, and the clamp is seated differently each time it is fitted.
6	
7	A clamp whose jaw faces match one nominal pipe diameter also obliges a technician to select the clamp to suit the pipe before working, and a jaw face of fixed curvature meets a pipe of a different diameter along an edge rather than over an area.
8	
9	An operator working with a quick acting latch further has little indication of how hard the clamp has been applied. The latch closes to the same position whether the jaws have only just reached the pipe or have been driven hard against it, so the feel of the latch does not report the load the clamp is carrying, and a reading of pipe diameter reports only the size of the pipe.
10	
11	There is accordingly a need for a split pipe clamp that can be fitted by hand around an in place pipe over a range of diameters, that advances several jaws onto the pipe together rather than one at a time, and that reports mechanically to the operator when the clamping load has reached the intended range.
12

Pipework in process plants, buildings, vehicles and drilling installations often has to be gripped by a device that cannot be threaded on from a free end of the pipe. Sensors, monitoring heads, marking tools, small actuators and conduit supports are attached to a run of pipe that is already installed. A clamp intended for that duty is therefore built as a split clamp: a frame that opens, is placed around the pipe transversely, and is closed again.

A split frame presents a mechanical problem that a one piece collar does not have, because the tightening motion has to be delivered to a frame that is divided. Where the grip is obtained by drawing the two frame halves toward one another so that the frame itself shrinks onto the pipe, the closing force enters the frame at the split line, and the grip that results depends on the closure hardware and on how far the halves have been drawn together.

Where instead the frame is fitted with jaws that are advanced against the pipe one at a time, the grip is taken away from the split line, but the jaws have to be balanced against one another by the operator. If one jaw is advanced further than the others, the pipe is pushed away from the axis of the frame, and the clamp is seated differently each time it is fitted.

A clamp whose jaw faces match one nominal pipe diameter also obliges a technician to select the clamp to suit the pipe before working, and a jaw face of fixed curvature meets a pipe of a different diameter along an edge rather than over an area.

An operator working with a quick acting latch further has little indication of how hard the clamp has been applied. The latch closes to the same position whether the jaws have only just reached the pipe or have been driven hard against it, so the feel of the latch does not report the load the clamp is carrying, and a reading of pipe diameter reports only the size of the pipe.

There is accordingly a need for a split pipe clamp that can be fitted by hand around an in place pipe over a range of diameters, that advances several jaws onto the pipe together rather than one at a time, and that reports mechanically to the operator when the clamping load has reached the intended range.

3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	Referring to FIG. 1, a split pipe clamp 10 comprises a first frame half 12 and a second frame half 14. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are each substantially semicircular, and together they define a frame that surrounds a pipe 20 when closed. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are joined at a hinge end of the frame by a hinge 16 and are releasably joined at a latch end of the frame, opposite the hinge end, by a releasable latch 18. Swinging the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16 opens the frame laterally, so that the split pipe clamp 10 can be placed around the pipe 20. 8	
9	The frame carries a mounting boss 66. The mounting boss 66 supports a sensor, a tool or a conduit on the split pipe clamp 10. The mounting boss 66 does not participate in synchronizing the jaw carriages 22.

In the following description, like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views. The described arrangement is one form of the invention and is not a limitation on the scope of the claims. Terms of orientation such as inward, outward, radial and circumferential are used with reference to a central axis of the closed frame, which in use is substantially coincident with the axis of the pipe being gripped.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a split pipe clamp 10 comprises a first frame half 12 and a second frame half 14. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are each substantially semicircular, and together they define a frame that surrounds a pipe 20 when closed. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are joined at a hinge end of the frame by a hinge 16 and are releasably joined at a latch end of the frame, opposite the hinge end, by a releasable latch 18. Swinging the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16 opens the frame laterally, so that the split pipe clamp 10 can be placed around the pipe 20. The split pipe clamp 10 and the pipe 20 together form an installed clamp assembly when the split pipe clamp 10 is closed and clamped on the pipe 20.

Three jaw carriages 22 are distributed circumferentially about the closed frame, as shown in FIG. 1.

The frame carries a mounting boss 66. The mounting boss 66 supports a sensor, a tool or a conduit on the split pipe clamp 10. The mounting boss 66 does not participate in synchronizing the jaw carriages 22.

Jaw carriages and jaw pads

Referring to FIG. 2, each jaw carriage 22 is slidable in a respective radial guide 24 of the frame. The radial guide 24 constrains the jaw carriage 22 to travel along a radial path toward and away from the central axis of the closed frame.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a jaw pad 26 that is mounted on the jaw carriage 22 for pivoting movement and that presents a concave bearing surface toward the central axis of the closed frame. Because the jaw pad 26 pivots relative to the jaw carriage 22, the jaw pad 26 bears on the pipe 20 without requiring a tool specific pipe diameter.

A carriage spring 42 biases each jaw carriage 22 outward, away from the central axis of the closed frame. When the releasable latch 18 is released, the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22 outward and lift the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened.

The segmented cam ring

A cam ring 30 is retained in an annular guide 36 of the frame. The annular guide 36, shown in FIG. 2, retains the cam ring 30 while allowing the cam ring 30 to rotate through a limited stroke about the central axis of the closed frame.

The mounting boss 66 stands on the frame outside the annular guide 36, as shown in FIG. 2.

The cam ring 30 is segmented. Referring to FIG. 3, the cam ring 30 comprises a first cam-ring segment 32 and a second cam-ring segment 34. The first cam-ring segment 32 is carried by the first frame half 12 and the second cam-ring segment 34 is carried by the second frame half 14, each segment being retained by the frame half that carries it. Each segment accordingly stays with its own frame half when the frame is opened, and the frame halves can be swung apart without dismantling the drive.

The first cam-ring segment 32 has a first hinge-end drive face 44 and a first latch-end drive face 48. The second cam-ring segment 34 has a second hinge-end drive face 46 and a second latch-end drive face 50. The first hinge-end drive face 44 and the second hinge-end drive face 46 are complementary to one another, and the first latch-end drive face 48 and the second latch-end drive face 50 are complementary to one another. Closing the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 brings the first hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the second hinge-end drive face 46 at the hinge end and brings the first latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the second latch-end drive face 50 at the latch end, and thereby couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 so that they rotate together as one cam ring 30 about the central axis of the closed frame.

In the closed frame each pair of complementary drive faces transmits circumferential drive from one cam-ring segment to the other, and the complementary drive faces separate when the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are swung apart about the hinge 16.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a follower 40 that is received in a respective oblique slot 38 of the cam ring 30. The follower 40 and the oblique slot 38 are shown in FIG. 2. Each oblique slot 38 is inclined to the circumferential direction of the cam ring 30, so that rotation of the cam ring 30 through the limited stroke displaces the follower 40, and with it the jaw carriage 22, along the radial guide 24. The oblique slots 38 are arranged so that rotation of the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke produces the same inward travel at every jaw carriage 22. The inward travel of the three jaw carriages 22 is thereby synchronized.

The latch drive

The releasable latch 18 carries a wedge 52, as shown in FIG. 4. Moving the releasable latch 18 drives the wedge 52 against a ring drive face 54 of the cam ring 30, shown in FIG. 3, and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke.

The releasable latch 18 has a first position and a second position. In the first position the releasable latch 18 holds the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 around the pipe 20 without clamping the pipe 20. The second position is an over-center position, in which the releasable latch 18 has driven the wedge 52 and the cam ring 30 and clamps the pipe 20.

Referring again to FIG. 4, the releasable latch 18 comprises a latch handle 56, a latch housing 58 and a force-limiting spring stack 62. The force-limiting spring stack 62 lies in a drive path between the latch handle 56 and the wedge 52.

Once all of the jaw pads 26 have contacted the pipe 20, further movement of the latch handle 56 toward the over-center position compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62 rather than forcing one jaw pad 26 farther than the others. The latch travel that remains after contact is therefore taken up by the force-limiting spring stack 62.

An indicator pin 64 is visible on the releasable latch 18 and moves relative to a fixed edge 60 of the latch housing 58 when the force-limiting spring stack 62 enters a predetermined compression range. The position of the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60 is a mechanical report that the split pipe clamp 10 is loaded within that range. The indicator pin 64 reports clamp loading and does not measure the diameter of the pipe 20.

Installation and removal

To install the split pipe clamp 10, an operator opens the releasable latch 18 and swings the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 20 and closes them, which brings the first hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the second hinge-end drive face 46 and the first latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the second latch-end drive face 50, and so couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 into a single cam ring 30. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the first position, in which the frame halves are held around the pipe 20 without clamping. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the over-center position. The wedge 52 bears on the ring drive face 54 and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke, the oblique slots 38 advance all of the jaw carriages 22 inward together, and the jaw pads 26 pivot and seat on the pipe 20. Latch travel remaining after the jaw pads 26 seat compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62, and the operator observes the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60.

To remove the split pipe clamp 10, the operator releases the releasable latch 18. The force-limiting spring stack 62 unloads and the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22, lifting the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are then swung apart about the hinge 16, and the first hinge-end drive face 44, the second hinge-end drive face 46, the first latch-end drive face 48 and the second latch-end drive face 50 separate so that the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 travel with their own frame halves. The split pipe clamp 10 is reusable.

The essential relationship of the arrangement described here is that closure of the frame halves couples the cam-ring segments, that travel of the releasable latch 18 drives the coupled cam ring 30, that the oblique slots 38 synchronize the radial travel of the jaw carriages 22, and that the force-limiting spring stack 62 accommodates the remaining latch travel. The features described above may be combined in ways other than those expressly set out, and modifications within the understanding of a person skilled in the art fall within the scope of the claims that follow.

Numerals 10–66 each denote exactly one part across the numerals table, description, and briefs; the hinge-end faces 44/46 sit at the left junction and the latch-end faces 48/50 at the right junction consistently across FIGS. 1–3; no section lines are used, and no drafting notes, placeholders, or open questions remain.

Reviewed input/disclosure.md, input/conversation.md (one USER passage, identical in substance to the disclosure), input/brief.md, draft sections 01-10, draft/numerals.md, and figures/FIG-1.md through FIG-4.md.

Ledger: every limitation of claims 1-17, every numbered part (10-66), and substantially all description and summary text trace to affirmative USER language. Specifically traced: semicircular frame halves joined by a hinge at one end and a releasable latch at the other; three jaw carriages distributed about the closed frame, each sliding in a radial guide and carrying a pivoting concave jaw pad that bears on a pipe "without requiring a tool-specific pipe diameter"; carriage springs biasing each carriage outward on release; a segmented cam ring retained in an annular guide with one segment carried by each frame half; complementary drive faces at the hinge and latch ends that couple the segments on closure so they move as one ring; a follower on each carriage received in a respective oblique slot; a wedge driven by the latch against a drive face of the cam ring, rotating the coupled ring through a limited stroke; oblique slots converting that rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three carriages; first (holding) and second over-center latch positions; a force-limiting spring stack between latch handle and wedge taking up travel after all pads contact; a visible indicator pin moving relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing at a predetermined compression range and reporting load rather than diameter; the install and remove sequences (supporting method claims 14-17); the optional mounting boss outside the annular guide for a sensor, tool or conduit that does not participate in synchronization (claims 8, 13, 17); and the installed-clamp-assembly combination of claim 11. The Background is prior-art characterization and is outside this ledger. draft/02 and draft/03 ("Not applicable.") match the brief's "No priority claim. No federally sponsored research or development."

Internal consistency: numerals 10-66 each denote one part throughout the numerals table, description, and briefs; numeral 28 is unused, which is permissible. Hinge-end faces 44/46 are placed at the left junction and latch-end faces 48/50 at the right junction, consistent with the hinge at the left break and the latch at the right break in FIG. 1 and the divisions in FIGS. 2-3. Claim terminology ("ring drive face", "carriage spring", "limited stroke", "over-center", "predetermined compression range") matches the description verbatim; claim antecedents are in order. No section lines exist, so no repeated section designation is required. No drafting notes, placeholders, open questions, unresolved alternatives, or internal comments remain, and neither the description nor the Brief Description contains "by way of example", "any closed outline", or any other text added to justify a renderer's generic choice.

Five findings, all in the figure briefs and their consistency with the text:

1. (critical) FIG-4 makes the wedge's inclined lower face contact an arcuate band expressly identified as "frame structure". The source has the wedge bearing only on a drive face of the cam ring, and the detailed description says the wedge 52 bears on ring drive face 54 of cam ring 30. The brief therefore asserts an undisclosed contact topology and a taper direction on a functional face, and contradicts the text.

2. (critical) FIG-4 has the indicator rod "standing on the upper end of the stack of springs". No source passage describes how the indicator pin is driven; the disclosure says only that it is visible and moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the stack enters a predetermined compression range. The depicted joint is an undisclosed connection, and because the handle's inner end acts at that same stack top, it also makes pin motion track handle travel rather than stack compression.

3. (major) FIG-3 places the ring drive face "clear of the junctions", a circumferential position statement about a functional face with no source support, and in tension with the wedge being carried by the latch at the latch end (which FIG. 1 puts at a junction).

4. (minor) FIG-4 draws the frame band beneath the latch housing as continuous, while FIG. 1 shows the latch straddling the right break between the two halves; the enlarged view of that same region should show the break.

5. (minor) The Brief Description of FIG. 2 lists only the annular guide, jaw carriages and mounting boss, although the detailed description cites FIG. 2 for oblique slot 38, follower 40 and carriage spring 42, and the brief also draws the cam ring band and jaw pads.

No unsupported optional embodiment, variant, material, operating condition, or result was found in the application text; the only untraced matter is the figure-brief geometry above, each with a removal-based fix that leaves the claims and description unchanged.

findings.detail: The brief defines the lower band as frame structure ("A plain arcuate band across the lower part of the drawing area representing frame structure") and then makes the wedge's inclined working face contact that band. structured_output.summary:
Reviewed input/disclosure.md, input/conversation.md (one USER passage, identical in substance to the disclosure), input/brief.md, draft sections 01-10, draft/numerals.md, and figures/FIG-1.md through FIG-4.md.

Ledger: every limitation of claims 1-17, every numbered part (10-66), and substantially all description and summary text trace to affirmative USER language. Specifically traced: semicircular frame halves joined by a hinge at one end and a releasable latch at the other; three jaw carriages distributed about the closed frame, each sliding in a radial guide and carrying a pivoting concave jaw pad that bears on a pipe "without requiring a tool-specific pipe diameter"; carriage springs biasing each carriage outward on release; a segmented cam ring retained in an annular guide with one segment carried by each frame half; complementary drive faces at the hinge and latch ends that couple the segments on closure so they move as one ring; a follower on each carriage received in a respective oblique slot; a wedge driven by the latch against a drive face of the cam ring, rotating the coupled ring through a limited stroke; oblique slots converting that rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three carriages; first (holding) and second over-center latch positions; a force-limiting spring stack between latch handle and wedge taking up travel after all pads contact; a visible indicator pin moving relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing at a predetermined compression range and reporting load rather than diameter; the install and remove sequences (supporting method claims 14-17); the optional mounting boss outside the annular guide for a sensor, tool or conduit that does not participate in synchronization (claims 8, 13, 17); and the installed-clamp-assembly combination of claim 11. The Background is prior-art characterization and is outside this ledger. draft/02 and draft/03 ("Not applicable.") match the brief's "No priority claim. No federally sponsored research or development."

Internal consistency: numerals 10-66 each denote one part throughout the numerals table, description, and briefs; numeral 28 is unused, which is permissible. Hinge-end faces 44/46 are placed at the left junction and latch-end faces 48/50 at the right junction, consistent with the hinge at the left break and the latch at the right break in FIG. 1 and the divisions in FIGS. 2-3. Claim terminology ("ring drive face", "carriage spring", "limited stroke", "over-center", "predetermined compression range") matches the description verbatim; claim antecedents are in order. No section lines exist, so no repeated section designation is required. No drafting notes, placeholders, open questions, unresolved alternatives, or internal comments remain, and neither the description nor the Brief Description contains "by way of example", "any closed outline", or any other text added to justify a renderer's generic choice.

Five findings, all in the figure briefs and their consistency with the text:

1. (critical) FIG-4 makes the wedge's inclined lower face contact an arcuate band expressly identified as "frame structure". The source has the wedge bearing only on a drive face of the cam ring, and the detailed description says the wedge 52 bears on ring drive face 54 of cam ring 30. The brief therefore asserts an undisclosed contact topology and a taper direction on a functional face, and contradicts the text.

2. (critical) FIG-4 has the indicator rod "standing on the upper end of the stack of springs". No source passage describes how the indicator pin is driven; the disclosure says only that it is visible and moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the stack enters a predetermined compression range. The depicted joint is an undisclosed connection, and because the handle's inner end acts at that same stack top, it also makes pin motion track handle travel rather than stack compression.

3. (major) FIG-3 places the ring drive face "clear of the junctions", a circumferential position statement about a functional face with no source support, and in tension with the wedge being carried by the latch at the latch end (which FIG. 1 puts at a junction).

4. (minor) FIG-4 draws the frame band beneath the latch housing as continuous, while FIG. 1 shows the latch straddling the right break between the two halves; the enlarged view of that same region should show the break.

5. (minor) The Brief Description of FIG. 2 lists only the annular guide, jaw carriages and mounting boss, although the detailed description cites FIG. 2 for oblique slot 38, follower 40 and carriage spring 42, and the brief also draws the cam ring band and jaw pads.

No unsupported optional embodiment, variant, material, operating condition, or result was found in the application text; the only untraced matter is the figure-brief geometry above, each with a removal-based fix that leaves the claims and description unchanged.

findings.title: FIG. 4 brief attaches the indicator rod to the top of the spring stack, a connection absent from the source

The source discloses only that the pin is visible and moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the stack enters a predetermined compression range; it never states how the pin is mounted or driven.
